5.3.1.architect: SPACE operates as a single-user CLI and lightweight web server, which fundamentally shapes its concurrency model. The engine in `src/engine/core.ts` uses an in-memory `Map<string, SessionState>` — there's no shared state between sessions, no locks, no transaction isolation. The `SpaceInstance` closure captures everything by reference, making it a monolith by design. The web server in `web/server.mjs` wraps this same engine in HTTP handlers with manual routing (`matchRoute`), which is fine for single-tab usage but would break under concurrent browser tabs accessing the same session — there's no optimistic locking on `SessionState` mutations. The `StorageProvider` interface in `src/storage/types.ts` defines pure CRUD with no concurrency primitives; `FileSystemStorage` uses synchronous `writeFileSync` which serializes writes at the OS level. The dependency graph traversal in `question-router.ts` is O(V+E) with V=7 series and ~10 edges — effectively constant time. The real latency bottleneck is LLM API calls (1-5s) via the `LLMProvider.complete()` interface, which are properly async and don't block the event loop. For the CLI path, `src/cli/tui.ts` uses a `readline` loop that blocks on user input — inherently single-threaded and single-user. The architecture trades concurrency for simplicity: no need for worker threads, no need for request queuing, no need for distributed state. If team collaboration were needed, the `StorageProvider` abstraction would be the seam to introduce a shared backing store with appropriate locking.
5.3.1.practitioner: The throughput profile is simple: SPACE handles one question submission at a time, with `submitAnswer()` in `core.ts` calling `setAnswer()` → `accumulateArtifacts()` → `advanceToNextQuestion()` synchronously. Each operation is sub-millisecond. The `auto_save_interval_ms` (default 10000ms) in `SpaceConfig` (`src/config/defaults.ts`) governs periodic persistence — `FileSystemStorage.createSession()` and `updateSession()` use `writeFileSync`, which blocks the Node event loop for ~1-5ms per write on typical hardware. The web server at `web/server.mjs` creates a single `SpaceInstance` via `createSpace()` at startup, storing it in module scope — concurrent HTTP requests to the same session will race on in-memory `SessionState`. The `exportToFiles()` function in `src/export/index.ts` writes sequentially with `mkdirSync` + `writeFileSync`, processing formats one at a time. The intelligence layer (`src/intelligence/index.ts`) runs `scoreCompleteness`, `detectContradictions`, `generateRecommendations` synchronously — each is O(n) on answer count, where n ≤ 335. Latency target: <100ms for all local operations (confirmed by the fact that `question-router.ts` does linear scans over small arrays). Memory footprint: `SessionState` with 335 answers at ~100 bytes each ≈ 33KB per session; the `Map<string, SessionState>` in core keeps all sessions loaded. Practical ceiling: the system is I/O-bound on user input (CLI) or LLM API (auto-fill), never CPU-bound.
5.3.1.strategist: SPACE's performance characteristics are ideal for its market position as a local developer tool. The zero-latency local operations (question routing, answer recording, artifact extraction) create the perception of an instant tool — critical for developer adoption where any perceived lag kills workflow integration. The 1-5 second LLM latency for auto-fill is acceptable because it's positioned as an enhancement, not the core flow. The single-user model eliminates an entire class of operational costs: no need for horizontal scaling, load balancers, session replication, or rate limiting. This keeps the tool free to run (no server costs beyond LLM API calls), which is a significant competitive advantage against SaaS specification tools like Notion, Confluence, or AI-assisted alternatives that charge per-seat. The performance profile also enables offline-first usage with Ollama as the LLM backend — a differentiator for enterprise users in air-gapped environments. Success metric: users should never notice the system's local operations. If question-to-artifact latency exceeds 200ms, investigate the `accumulateArtifacts()` call chain in `src/data/artifact-mapping.ts`. The current architecture doesn't need optimization — it needs protection from over-engineering. Don't add Redis, don't add worker threads, don't add caching layers for a 33KB session file.
5.3.1.critic: The single-user, single-session assumption is baked deep into `createSpace()` — it returns a closure over a single `Map<string, SessionState>` with no isolation. If `web/server.mjs` receives two concurrent POST requests to the same session endpoint, the second read will see stale data from the first write (classic read-modify-write race). The `FileSystemStorage` uses synchronous file I/O, which is correct for the single-user CLI but creates an architectural mismatch with the async web server — `writeFileSync` blocks the entire Node event loop during disk writes. This won't matter at current scale, but it's a latent correctness issue: if two export requests arrive simultaneously, both block on sequential `writeFileSync` calls in `exportToFiles()`. The `auto_save_interval_ms` timer in `core.ts` fires independently of the web request cycle — there's no guarantee that an auto-save won't race with a concurrent HTTP request modifying the same session. The dependency graph is small (7 nodes, ~10 edges) making traversal negligible, but the `getCurrentQuestion` function in `question-router.ts` does a linear scan of `round.open_ended` to find unanswered questions — technically O(n) per round, not O(1) lookup. This is fine at 67 questions but represents a design choice that assumes small datasets. The real risk isn't performance — it's that nobody has defined the concurrency contract. What happens if the CLI and web server run against the same `projects_dir`? The `FileSystemStorage` provides no file locking.

5.3.2.architect: SPACE's data model is compact by design. The `FrameworkDefinition` (67 questions, 7 series, 25 rounds) is static JSON loaded once at initialization via `loadFrameworkFromV1()` in `src/data/framework-loader.ts`. Session state (`SessionState` in `src/types/index.ts`) grows linearly with answers: each `AnswerEntry` stores `question_id`, `series_id`, `round`, `open_ended_text`, `multi_choice_id`, and metadata — roughly 100-200 bytes per answer. A complete session (67 answers) is ~10-15KB of JSON. The `ArtifactDictionary` accumulates derived values from answers — typically 20-50 artifacts at ~500 bytes each, totaling ~25KB. Snapshots (created at round/series boundaries via `snapshot-manager.ts`) duplicate the full session state, creating a copy-on-write pattern. With 5 series × 3 rounds = ~15 snapshots per completed session, plus manual snapshots, storage grows to ~200KB per session. The `StorageProvider` interface (`src/storage/types.ts`) defines no TTL, no compaction, no partitioning — data accumulates linearly. The `FileSystemStorage` organizes data as `{baseDir}/{project_id}/sessions/{session_id}/state.json` with separate snapshot directories, creating a natural partition boundary at the project level. Growth rate is strictly linear: N projects × M sessions × ~200KB. At 100 projects × 10 sessions, total storage is ~200MB — well within single-node capacity indefinitely.
5.3.2.practitioner: Concrete storage accounting: `SessionState` contains `session: SessionMeta` (~200B), `answers: Record<string, AnswerEntry>` (67 entries × 150B = ~10KB), `progress: ProgressState` (~300B), `artifacts: ArtifactDictionary` (~25KB), and optional `llm_metadata` (~100B). Total per session: ~36KB JSON. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` writes this as pretty-printed JSON (`JSON.stringify(session, null, 2)`) with a 2x size multiplier — so ~72KB on disk. Snapshots duplicate the full state: `Snapshot.state` is the complete `SessionState`, adding another ~72KB per snapshot. With `auto_save_interval_ms` at 10000ms (from `src/config/defaults.ts`), a 30-minute session generates ~180 auto-saves, but since snapshots only trigger at round/series completion (`'round_complete' | 'series_complete' | 'manual' | 'auto'` per `types/index.ts`), actual snapshot count is ~15-20 per completed session. The `projects_dir` default is `~/.space/projects/`, and the `SQLiteStorage` adapter (`src/storage/sqlite.ts`) is available but not the default. Growth projection: a team of 5 developers × 50 projects × 3 sessions × 72KB = ~54MB annually. Growth rate: sub-MB/month for typical individual usage. No compaction needed; no archival strategy needed; no partitioning needed.
5.3.2.strategist: The data volume profile makes SPACE essentially free to operate from a storage perspective. The entire framework definition is ~50KB. A completed specification session produces ~200KB of structured data. Exported specifications (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML) are ~10-50KB each. Total data footprint for a year of active use: under 10MB. This has zero cost implications — no cloud storage, no database licensing, no backup infrastructure. The simplicity of JSON-on-filesystem storage also means zero operational burden: users can back up projects by copying a directory, share sessions via email, and version-control outputs with Git. The `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) already supports auto-commit with `[space]` prefix. For market positioning, this small footprint enables 'spec-as-code' workflows where specification files live alongside source code in the same repository. The growth rate analysis matters for team adoption: at 50MB/year per developer, an organization of 1000 developers generates 50GB/year of specification data — trivially manageable with existing infrastructure. Success metric: storage should never be a topic of conversation. If users start asking about disk usage, something has gone wrong in the architecture (probably unbounded snapshot creation or accumulated exports). The `SQLiteStorage` adapter exists for future queryability needs but should remain opt-in.
5.3.2.critic: The 'trivially small' data profile masks a real issue: there's no data lifecycle management at all. `FileSystemStorage.deleteSession()` exists but is never called automatically. Snapshots accumulate without bound — the `saveSnapshot()` method in `snapshot-manager.ts` creates a new snapshot file on every trigger with no deduplication and no pruning. If a user completes 5 series × 3 rounds × 2 (round + series snapshots) = 30 snapshots per session, each at 72KB, that's 2.1MB of snapshot data per session. Over 100 sessions, that's 210MB of snapshot-only data — still manageable, but it's 10x the session state itself. The `pretty-printed JSON.stringify` doubles on-disk size compared to minified JSON — an unnecessary overhead for files that are only read by the application, never by humans. The `ProjectArchive` type in `types/index.ts` bundles sessions and exports together, creating potential for data duplication if archives are exported alongside source sessions. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter (`src/storage/sqlite.ts`) provides better query performance for cross-session analytics but isn't the default, creating a fragmented storage story. The `exportToFiles()` function writes to `output_dir` with no cleanup — repeated exports accumulate files. There's no `.gitignore` awareness: exported files in the project directory would pollute repositories. Growth projections assume ideal usage; in practice, users will create abandoned sessions, duplicate projects, and accumulate exports that they never clean up.

5.3.3.architect: SPACE's availability model is best-effort by design. As a local tool running on a single developer machine, 'uptime' is equivalent to 'is Node.js running and does the filesystem work.' There's no server to deploy, no load balancer to monitor, no database to keep healthy. The `createSpace()` factory in `src/engine/core.ts` initializes synchronously — if it fails, it throws and the process exits. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` uses synchronous `writeFileSync`/`readFileSync`, which will throw on permission errors or disk-full conditions but won't corrupt data (atomic writes at the OS level for files < 4KB). The `Snapshot` system (`src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts`) provides automatic snapshots at round and series completion boundaries, creating implicit recovery points. If the process crashes mid-session, the latest snapshot preserves progress up to the last completed round. The `SpaceConfig.auto_save_interval_ms` provides an additional safety net — even without explicit snapshots, auto-saves create a rolling backup. For disaster recovery: sessions live in `~/.space/projects/` as plain JSON files. Backup = copy directory. Recovery = restore files. The `exportArchive()` method in `StorageProvider` creates a self-contained `ProjectArchive` bundle for portable backup. There's no cloud sync, no replication, no automated backup — these are explicitly out of scope for a local tool. The event system (`SpaceEvent` types) provides hooks for external monitoring but ships with no built-in monitoring integration.
5.3.3.practitioner: Reliability mechanisms in the SPACE codebase: (1) The `snapshot-manager.ts` creates snapshots with trigger types `'round_complete' | 'series_complete' | 'manual' | 'auto'` — each snapshot stores the full `SessionState` in a separate file, providing crash recovery up to the last snapshot boundary. (2) `auto_save_interval_ms` (default 10000ms from `src/config/defaults.ts`) triggers periodic persistence via the engine's save mechanism. (3) `FileSystemStorage` uses `writeFileSync` which is synchronous and blocking — for files under 4KB (typical session state), this is effectively atomic on most filesystems (ext4, NTFS, APFS). (4) The `SessionMeta.status` field tracks `'created' | 'in_progress' | 'completed' | 'abandoned'` — sessions interrupted by crash remain `'in_progress'` and can be resumed via `resumeSession()`. (5) The `exportArchive()`/`importArchive()` pair on `StorageProvider` enables full project backup as a single JSON blob. What's missing: no write-ahead log, no fsync guarantees (writes go through page cache), no file locking (concurrent CLI + web access to the same session could corrupt state), no corruption detection (no checksums in `SessionState` or `Snapshot`). The SQLite adapter adds WAL mode and transactional writes but is not the default. Practically, for a single-user tool, the combination of auto-save + snapshots + filesystem atomic writes provides adequate durability. Recovery: find the latest `state.json` or snapshot, load it, and resume.
5.3.3.strategist: SPACE's availability model is deliberately minimal: best-effort, no SLA, no formal DR plan. This is the correct choice for a local developer tool. The 'uptime' equivalent is 'does the tool work when I need it?' — and the answer is yes, as long as Node.js is installed and the filesystem is accessible. The economic argument is compelling: zero infrastructure cost for availability, zero operational overhead, zero on-call burden. The snapshot system provides automatic recovery points without requiring users to understand backup concepts. The `ProjectArchive` format creates a portable, human-readable backup that can be shared, emailed, or committed to version control. For enterprise customers who need more, the `SQLiteStorage` adapter provides transactional durability with WAL mode, and the `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) enables automatic version control of specification data. The disaster recovery story is 'copy the ~/.space directory' — simple enough that any developer can do it without documentation. Success metric: no user has ever lost work due to a SPACE bug. The auto-save + snapshot combination makes this achievable. For market positioning: 'your data lives on your machine, not in our cloud' is a strong privacy/security selling point for enterprise adoption.
5.3.3.critic: The 'best-effort' label is honest but understates real risks. The `FileSystemStorage` uses `writeFileSync` without explicit `fsync` — data is written to the OS page cache but may not be on disk for up to 30 seconds on Linux (controlled by `dirty_expire_centisecs`). A power loss within this window loses the most recent auto-save. The snapshot system mitigates this: snapshots are written after round/series completion, not on every answer, so a crash between auto-saves loses at most one round of progress. However, `writeFileSync` on a file that already exists is NOT atomic — if the process crashes during the write, the file may be partially written (corrupted). The `readFileSync` in `getSession()` would then fail with a JSON parse error. There's no recovery mechanism for corrupted session files — no backup rotation, no checksum validation, no fallback to the previous snapshot. The `ProjectArchive` export is the only portable backup, but it's opt-in and manual. The snapshot files duplicate the full session state (no incremental snapshots), so a corrupted snapshot doesn't help recover from a corrupted session file — you'd need an earlier snapshot. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter fixes the atomicity issue with WAL mode but isn't the default, creating a reliability gap. The `abandoned` status exists but is never automatically set — interrupted sessions appear as `in_progress` indefinitely, with no automated cleanup or user notification.

5.3.4.architect: SPACE uses vertical scaling exclusively — all state lives in a single Node.js process. The `SpaceInstance` closure in `src/engine/core.ts` holds `sessions: Map<string, SessionState>` in memory, which scales with available RAM. A single session is ~36KB of state; even 10,000 concurrent sessions would consume ~360MB — well within a single process's capacity. The `StorageProvider` interface (`src/storage/types.ts`) is the only abstraction that could support horizontal scaling, but the current `FileSystemStorage` implementation assumes local filesystem access with no distributed coordination. The web server in `web/server.mjs` is a single `createServer` instance with no clustering, no worker processes, no process manager. This is appropriate: the tool serves one user's browser, not a production traffic load. The `LLMProvider` interface in `src/llm/types.ts` is stateless per-request — each `complete()` call is independent, making it trivially parallelizable if needed. The dependency graph traversal and artifact extraction are CPU-bound but operate on fixed-size data (7 nodes, 67 questions) — parallelization would add complexity without benefit. The architecture has no horizontal scaling seams: no session partitioning, no shared-nothing design, no event sourcing. This is a feature, not a limitation — the tool's scope doesn't require it.
5.3.4.practitioner: Concrete scaling analysis: The `createSpace()` function allocates a single `SpaceInstance` with a `Map<string, SessionState>`. Memory per session: `SessionState` ≈ 36KB (answers) + `ArtifactDictionary` ≈ 25KB + snapshot references = ~61KB. Node.js overhead per Map entry: ~100 bytes. At 1000 sessions in memory: ~61MB. The `FileSystemStorage` at `src/storage/filesystem.ts` performs synchronous reads with `readFileSync` and writes with `writeFileSync` — both block the event loop. For the web server path, each HTTP request to `GET /api/session/:id` calls `storage.getSession()`, which reads `state.json` from disk. At 100 requests/sec with 1KB session files, disk I/O is ~100KB/sec — negligible for any modern SSD. The `writeFileSync` calls in `exportToFiles()` (`src/export/index.ts`) are sequential: for N export formats, N sequential writes. The `createProvider()` factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` returns a new provider instance per session, but providers like `OpenAIProvider` are stateless beyond holding an API key. The `execSync` in `GitIntegration.run()` (`src/integration/git.ts`) blocks for up to 10 seconds — this is the only potentially problematic blocking call. Vertical scaling ceiling: the system becomes disk-I/O-bound long before CPU or memory limits. Practical recommendation: don't add clustering, don't add worker threads — the complexity isn't justified.
5.3.4.strategist: Vertical scaling is the right choice for SPACE's market position. The tool runs on a developer's machine — a laptop with 8-16GB RAM and an SSD. The entire system (engine + storage + exports + LLM integration) fits comfortably in <200MB of RAM and <100MB of disk. There's no economic case for horizontal scaling: no cloud infrastructure, no server fleet, no load balancer to maintain. The vertical-only model means SPACE is deployable everywhere Node.js runs: Windows, macOS, Linux, WSL2, Docker containers, CI/CD pipelines. This universality is a competitive advantage over server-bound alternatives. The scalability question is actually a non-question for the current product scope — but answering it well in the generated specification demonstrates understanding. For the specification output, the strategist should emphasize that vertical scaling is a deliberate architectural choice aligned with the product's local-first philosophy. If the product evolves to include team features (shared specs, collaborative editing), the scaling model would shift — but that's a different product. Success metric: SPACE should run smoothly on a 5-year-old MacBook Air with 8GB RAM. If it doesn't, the scaling model has failed. The current architecture achieves this. Don't add Redis, don't add message queues, don't add process managers.
5.3.4.critic: The vertical scaling assumption creates a single point of failure that nobody addresses directly. If the Node.js process crashes, all in-memory sessions are lost (mitigated by snapshots, but snapshots only capture completed rounds, not in-progress answers). The `FileSystemStorage` synchronous I/O model is correct for single-user but creates a hard ceiling: the web server can't handle concurrent requests efficiently because each request blocks on disk reads. The `createServer` callback in `web/server.mjs` is async, but the underlying storage calls are sync — this creates a mismatch where the event loop appears free but is actually blocked during file operations. The `execSync` in `GitIntegration.run()` is particularly concerning: it blocks the entire event loop for up to 10 seconds per git operation. If auto-commit is triggered during a web request, the request will hang. There's no process isolation between the CLI and web server when they share the same `projects_dir` — two processes writing to the same session file will corrupt it. The `SQLiteStorage` adapter adds better concurrency control (WAL mode allows concurrent reads) but still assumes a single process. The real scaling concern isn't throughput — it's the absence of any documentation or enforcement of single-process access constraints. Users might accidentally run both CLI and web server simultaneously against the same data directory.

5.3.5.architect: SPACE's security model is minimal by design, appropriate for a local development tool. The attack surface is small: (1) No network listener by default — the CLI path has no HTTP server. The web server (`web/server.mjs`) binds to localhost only with permissive CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`). (2) No user input processing beyond text storage — answer text is stored as-is in `SessionState.answers[key].open_ended_text` with no sanitization, no HTML escaping, no SQL injection risk (no SQL in the filesystem adapter). (3) No authentication — the `StorageProvider` interface has no auth concepts. The web server has no login, no tokens, no session management. This is correct for localhost-only usage. (4) The `LLMProvider.complete()` method sends user answers to external LLM APIs over HTTPS — this is the only sensitive data transmission. API keys are stored in `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key`, which lives in the application's config but is not encrypted at rest. (5) The `FileSystemStorage` relies on OS filesystem permissions for access control — data files are readable by the running user. There's no encryption at rest, no audit logging, no access control beyond OS-level file permissions. The `Snapshot` type stores full `SessionState` snapshots as plaintext files. For compliance: SPACE processes no PII beyond voluntarily entered text, no financial data, no health data — no GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2, or PCI-DSS obligations apply.
5.3.5.practitioner: Security-relevant code paths: (1) LLM API calls — `OpenAIProvider`, `AnthropicProvider`, `GeminiProvider`, `MistralProvider` in `src/llm/providers/` make HTTPS requests with API keys in headers. Keys are passed via `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key` from `src/config/defaults.ts` defaults or user configuration. No key rotation, no key storage encryption, no key validation beyond checking existence before fallback to `TemplateProvider`. (2) `web/server.mjs` — raw `http.createServer` with manual routing, no helmet, no rate limiting, no input validation middleware. Request bodies parsed via `JSON.parse` with a catch that silently returns `{}` on parse failure — this prevents crashes but could lead to unexpected behavior with malformed input. (3) `GitIntegration.run()` in `src/integration/git.ts` — uses `execSync` with `timeout: 10000` and `stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe']`, preventing stdout/stderr leaking to the terminal but allowing arbitrary git command execution based on `GitConfig`. The `commitMessagePrefix` field is user-controlled and passed directly to git commands — potential for command injection if it contains shell metacharacters (mitigated by `execSync` not using a shell, but still a code smell). (4) `FileSystemStorage` — `writeFileSync`/`readFileSync` with paths derived from `project_id` and `session_id` (both `randomUUID`-based) — no path traversal risk since IDs are generated internally. (5) Export formats (`src/export/formatters/`) — `html-exporter.ts` generates HTML from answer text; if answers contain `<script>` tags, exported HTML is vulnerable to stored XSS if opened in a browser. No HTML sanitization is applied to answer text before export.
5.3.5.strategist: SPACE's security posture is 'secure enough for a local tool' — which is the right level for its market positioning. The tool runs on a developer's machine, processes no sensitive data beyond what the user voluntarily enters, and has no network exposure beyond optional LLM API calls. The security story for enterprise buyers is actually strong: (1) No data leaves the machine unless the user explicitly enables LLM auto-fill. (2) Data lives in plaintext JSON files that can be audited, backed up, and version-controlled. (3) No third-party analytics, no telemetry, no phone-home behavior. (4) The `GitIntegration` class enables automatic version control of specification data, providing audit trails. For adoption strategy, this zero-telemetry, local-first model is a selling point for regulated industries (finance, healthcare, government) where SaaS tools face procurement barriers. The lack of encryption at rest is acceptable because the data (project specifications) is not inherently sensitive — it describes what a system should do, not who uses it. However, if users start storing credentials, API keys, or PII in their specification answers, the lack of encryption becomes a real concern. Success metric: zero security incidents attributable to SPACE's architecture. The current model achieves this by having minimal attack surface.
5.3.5.critic: The security model has several unaddressed risks that become real as the tool matures. (1) Stored XSS via exported HTML: `html-exporter.ts` renders answer text into HTML without sanitization. If a user writes `<script>alert(1)</script>` as an answer and exports to HTML, the resulting file executes arbitrary JavaScript when opened. This is a real vulnerability if exported specs are shared with non-technical stakeholders. (2) API key storage: `SpaceConfig.llm_api_key` is passed in memory and potentially persisted in config files with no encryption. The `createProvider()` factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` creates a new provider instance per session, but the key lives in the config object which persists for the process lifetime. (3) The web server's CORS policy (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) allows any website to make requests to the local server. If a user has the SPACE web server running and visits a malicious site, that site can read their session data via fetch requests to `localhost:8888`. This is a classic localhost CSRF/exfiltration attack. (4) `GitIntegration` commits specification data with no `.gitignore` awareness — users might accidentally push API keys or sensitive text embedded in their specification answers to public repositories. (5) No audit trail: the `SpaceEvent` system provides hooks but ships with no logging implementation. For a tool used in regulated environments, the absence of access logging and change history (beyond git) is a compliance gap. (6) The `FileSystemStorage` stores data as plaintext — no encryption at rest means any process with filesystem access can read specification data. For a local tool, this is acceptable, but it's worth documenting as a limitation.

5.4.1.architect: SPACE's integration architecture follows a hub-and-spoke model with the Engine as the hub. The Engine (`src/engine/core.ts`) exposes a `SpaceInstance` interface that CLI, web server, and any future consumers interact with. External integrations are isolated behind purpose-specific interfaces: (1) `LLMProvider` in `src/llm/types.ts` — a clean abstraction with `complete(params: CompletionParams): Promise<CompletionResult>`. The factory in `src/llm/factory.ts` selects from 7 provider implementations (`openai`, `anthropic`, `gemini`, `mistral`, `ollama`, `local`, `none`), each in its own file under `src/llm/providers/`. Adding a new LLM provider requires implementing the 3-method `LLMProvider` interface and adding a case to the switch in `createProvider()`. (2) `StorageProvider` in `src/storage/types.ts` — a 15-method CRUD interface for projects, sessions, snapshots, exports, and archives. Two implementations: `FileSystemStorage` (default, local JSON files) and `SQLiteStorage` (optional, transactional). The web server (`web/server.mjs`) wraps the engine in REST endpoints but doesn't interact with external systems directly. The `GitIntegration` class (`src/integration/git.ts`) wraps `git` CLI commands via `execSync` — it's not behind an interface, making it harder to mock or replace. The `export/index.ts` module provides 5 renderers (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, prompt) that are pure functions: `(session, artifacts, framework, format, name, opts) => ExportResult`. No databases, no message queues, no service meshes. The architecture's strength is interface-based extensibility; its weakness is that integrations are optional and can degrade silently (LLM fallback to TemplateProvider).
5.4.1.practitioner: Concrete integration surface area: (1) LLM providers — 5 HTTP integrations via `src/llm/providers/*.ts`. Each implements `LLMProvider.complete()` which returns `Promise<CompletionResult>`. OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral use their respective REST APIs; Ollama connects to `http://localhost:11434`. The `isAvailable()` method checks if the provider is reachable. (2) Git — `src/integration/git.ts` uses `execSync('git ...', { cwd, timeout: 10000 })` for: `init`, `status`, `commit`, `diff`, `log`, `branch`, `stash`. The `GitIntegration` constructor takes a `repoPath` and optional `GitConfig`. (3) npm registry — package published as `space-cli` per `package.json` `'bin': {'space': 'dist/cli/index.js'}`. (4) Web UI — `web/server.mjs` creates HTTP endpoints (`/api/framework`, `/api/projects`, `/api/session/:id`, etc.) consumed by `web/index.html` via `fetch()`. No WebSocket, no SSE, no streaming. (5) Filesystem — `FileSystemStorage` reads/writes JSON files; `exportToFiles()` writes export outputs to `output_dir`. All integration points use TypeScript interfaces (except Git). The `createProvider()` factory pattern in `src/llm/factory.ts` is the canonical extension point for adding new LLM backends. The `StorageProvider` interface is the extension point for alternative persistence backends. No API gateway, no service discovery, no integration testing framework for external dependencies.
5.4.1.strategist: SPACE's integration model is deliberately minimal — the tool is self-contained with optional external connections. This is a strategic advantage in the developer tooling market: zero mandatory integrations means zero setup friction. The npm-based distribution (`npm install -g space-cli`) is the primary channel, requiring only Node.js >= 18.0.0. The optional LLM integrations (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama) provide AI-powered features without making the tool dependent on any cloud service — the `null-provider.ts` and `template-provider.ts` ensure the tool works offline. The Git integration (`src/integration/git.ts`) adds version control awareness without requiring Git (graceful degradation via try/catch in `run()`). For market positioning, the 'bring your own LLM' strategy is powerful: it eliminates vendor lock-in, reduces operational costs (users pay API providers directly), and enables air-gapped usage via Ollama. The lack of mandatory integrations also means SPACE can be adopted incrementally — try it locally first, then add LLM auto-fill, then add Git auto-commit. Each integration is independently opt-in. The absence of database, message queue, or cloud dependencies means SPACE can be adopted in environments where procurement processes block SaaS tools. Success metric: 90% of new users should be running their first session within 5 minutes of installation, with zero integrations configured.
5.4.1.critic: The integration model has structural weaknesses that become apparent at scale. (1) The `GitIntegration` class uses `execSync` which blocks the event loop for up to 10 seconds — if auto-commit triggers during a web request, the request hangs. The class is also not behind an interface, making it impossible to mock in tests or swap for a Git library (like `simple-git` or `isomorphic-git`). (2) LLM provider fallback is silent: if `llm_api_key` is missing, `createProvider()` returns a `TemplateProvider` without any user notification — the user might think auto-fill is working when it's actually returning static templates. (3) The web server (`web/server.mjs`) has no streaming support — LLM responses that take 5 seconds produce no intermediate feedback. The `fetch()` calls in `web/index.html` block until the full response arrives. (4) The `StorageProvider` interface defines 15 methods but no event hooks — adding a new storage backend that needs to trigger side effects (e.g., webhooks, notifications) requires wrapping the entire interface. (5) The export system (`src/export/index.ts`) is synchronous — `exportToFiles()` blocks on `writeFileSync` for each format. For the web server path, large HTML exports would block the event loop. (6) No integration tests for LLM providers — the `isAvailable()` method is the only health check, and it's never called automatically. A misconfigured API key produces a runtime error during session processing, not during initialization. (7) The `package.json` lists `'lint': 'echo no linter configured'` — the tool ships with no code quality gate for integrations.

5.4.2.architect: SPACE's protocol landscape is intentionally narrow. The Engine-to-consumer communication happens through two channels: (1) Direct TypeScript function calls for CLI usage — `src/cli/index.ts` imports and calls `createSpace()` and engine methods directly. No serialization, no transport layer, no protocol overhead. The `SpaceInstance` interface in `src/engine/core.ts` is the contract. (2) REST/JSON over HTTP for the web server — `web/server.mjs` wraps the engine in endpoints using raw `http.createServer`. The protocol is simple: `GET` for reads, `POST` for mutations, JSON request/response bodies. No OpenAPI spec, no Swagger, no protocol versioning. LLM integrations use REST/JSON over HTTPS — each provider adapter (`openai-provider.ts`, `anthropic-provider.ts`, etc.) translates between the internal `CompletionParams` format and the provider's API format. The Ollama adapter uses `http://localhost:11434` REST API. Export formats are pure string transformations — no serialization protocols, just format-specific renderers that output text (JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML). Session persistence is JSON files on the filesystem — `JSON.stringify(session, null, 2)` for writes, `JSON.parse(readFileSync(...))` for reads. The `StorageProvider` interface defines the contract but not the transport — it's an in-process API, not a network protocol. There's no gRPC, no GraphQL, no WebSocket, no message queue, no event stream. This simplicity is a deliberate architectural choice.
5.4.2.practitioner: Protocol specifics in the codebase: (1) Web server REST API in `web/server.mjs`: `GET /api/framework` returns framework metadata as JSON; `GET /api/projects` lists projects; `POST /api/project` creates a project; `GET /api/session/:id` returns session state; `POST /api/session/:id/answer` submits an answer. Response format: `{ data: T }` for success, `{ error: string }` for failure. Content-Type: `application/json` for all responses. (2) LLM APIs: OpenAI uses `POST https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions` with `model`, `messages`, `temperature`, `max_tokens`. Anthropic uses `POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` with `model`, `messages`, `max_tokens`. Gemini uses `POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent`. Mistral uses `POST https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions` (OpenAI-compatible). Ollama uses `POST http://localhost:11434/api/generate`. All use JSON request/response over HTTPS (except Ollama which is HTTP). (3) Session persistence: `FileSystemStorage` reads/writes `state.json` files as `JSON.stringify(session, null, 2)`. No schema versioning in the file — `SessionMeta.framework_version` provides version context. (4) Export formats: JSON (`JSON.stringify`), Markdown (template string interpolation), YAML (`js-yaml` library or manual formatting), HTML (template literals), prompt (text extraction). All are synchronous string transformations. No binary formats, no compression, no streaming.
5.4.2.strategist: SPACE's protocol choices prioritize simplicity and developer familiarity. REST/JSON for the web API is the lowest-common-denominator protocol — every developer and every tool can consume it. The LLM API integrations use each provider's native REST format, which means adding a new provider requires understanding their specific API rather than fitting a generic abstraction. The lack of a formal API spec (no OpenAPI/Swagger) means the web API is undocumented beyond the source code — acceptable for a local tool used by developers who can read `web/server.mjs`, but a barrier for third-party integration. For the specification output, the strategist should note that REST/JSON is the right choice for the current scope: it's universally understood, trivially testable with `curl`, and compatible with any frontend framework. The absence of streaming (SSE or WebSocket) means LLM responses are buffered — users see a loading indicator, then the complete response. For the auto-fill feature, streaming would improve perceived latency but adds complexity. The file-based persistence (JSON on filesystem) enables 'spec-as-code' workflows where specification files live in Git alongside source code — a workflow pattern that resonates with developer audiences. The lack of gRPC, GraphQL, or binary protocols is correct: none of these would add value to a tool that processes 67 questions and writes ~10KB of text. Success metric: a developer can understand the entire API surface by reading `web/server.mjs` — currently achievable in 5 minutes.
5.4.2.critic: The protocol landscape is simple but has gaps that limit extensibility. (1) The REST API in `web/server.mjs` has no formal schema — no OpenAPI, no JSON Schema, no TypeScript types for request/response contracts. Changes to the API require reading the source code; there's no way to generate a client, validate requests, or detect breaking changes. The manual `matchRoute` function with regex-free string splitting is fragile and won't handle edge cases (double slashes, query parameters, encoded characters). (2) No protocol versioning — the `/api/` endpoints have no version prefix (`/api/v1/`). Any API change is a breaking change for existing web UI consumers. (3) LLM providers use different protocol flavors despite superficial similarities: Anthropic uses `system` as a top-level parameter, OpenAI puts it in the `messages` array, Gemini uses `contents` with role-based formatting. The adapter pattern in `src/llm/providers/` handles this but doesn't abstract the protocol differences — each adapter is a bespoke translation layer. (4) No streaming for LLM responses — the `CompletionResult` type in `src/llm/types.ts` returns a complete `text` string, not a stream. Users wait for the full response (1-5 seconds) with no incremental feedback. (5) The web server has no request body size limit — a malicious POST with a multi-megabyte body could exhaust memory. (6) Export formats use `JSON.stringify` for YAML compatibility checks but don't actually validate YAML output — the `yaml-exporter.ts` may produce invalid YAML for strings with special characters. (7) No content negotiation: the web server always returns JSON regardless of the `Accept` header.
